passages.title: The Card Under the Door
passages.text:
The card slides under Theo Brack's door at eleven at night, which is already strange, since nobody in this building visits after nine.  It is plain white and unlined, and it holds exactly six words in handwriting so neat it looks printed: You noticed the gap.  Come find out why.  Theo reads it four times before he understands that the gap means the loose floorboard in the third-floor hallway.  He has stepped over it every day for a year, because stepping on it makes a sound like a complaint.  Nobody else on this floor has ever mentioned it.  He has never mentioned it either.

He almost throws the card away, because a stranger who knows what you noticed and never said out loud is not a comforting thought at eleven at night.  Then he turns it over and finds an address on the back: the old Bellhaven Athenaeum, the library building three streets over.  It closed to the public two winters ago and has sat dark ever since.  Theo has walked past its boarded windows a hundred times without once wondering what was still inside.

He goes back the next afternoon, mostly because staying home and wondering is worse than any answer he might get.  The Athenaeum's front doors are chained, exactly as they have been for two years.  A side door under the fire escape stands open half an inch, as if somebody left it that way on purpose, confident nobody else would ever try it.  Theo stands on the step for a long moment.  Walking through that gap is a small thing.  It is also the first real decision he has made in longer than he wants to admit.

Inside, the dust is thinner than it should be for a building that has been empty two years, which means somebody has been walking these floors more recently than the chained doors suggest.  A woman is waiting at the bottom of a spiral staircase, arms folded, watching him arrive with an expression that is not quite a smile.  She introduces herself as Finch and says she keeps this place, though she does not say what this place is.

Finch does not ask why he came.  She asks what he noticed on the way in, then keeps asking, question after small question.  She asks about the chain that was not actually locked, the light under the door that nobody left on by accident, and the exact spot where the newer dust ended and the older dust began.  Theo answers every one, and only once he stops talking does he realize that he has been tested for twenty minutes and never once felt like he was being tested.  Finch tells him that noticing is the only qualification that has ever mattered here, and that the building goes a great deal deeper than the last hundred people who walked past it ever guessed.  Then she turns and starts down a second staircase, one Theo did not know was there, and does not look back to see if he is following, because by then she already knows he is.

passages.title: Two Empty Chairs
passages.text:
I count four chairs around Finch's table, and only two of them get used, which tells me something before anyone says a word.  I take the one nearest the door, because I like knowing where the door is, and a boy about my age takes the other one without asking whether it is taken.  He introduces himself as Theo, then seems to regret it immediately, like talking to a stranger is a skill he is still building.  I decide I like him better for that than I would have liked someone smooth.

Finch does not explain what this place is.  She sets a single photograph on the table between us: a glass disc, roughly the size of a coaster, etched with a pattern that curves in on itself like a shell.  She asks what we notice, and Theo says the pattern looks like a maze with no walls.  That is a better answer than mine would have been, because I was still counting the empty chairs.

I ask the question I actually care about.  Why are there two empty chairs?  Did two people quit, or have two people simply not arrived yet?  Finch says that is the correct question to have asked, though she does not answer it.  I have known her for eleven minutes, and I already understand that this is going to be a pattern.

She tells us the disc in the photograph has a name, the Threadglass, documented in three separate archives across two centuries.  Then it vanished from all three collections within the same decade.  Objects like that do not vanish on their own, she says.  Someone wanted it enough to risk being caught holding it, three times, in three different countries.  She wants to know if we want it back badly enough to take a much smaller risk than that.

Theo asks who has it now.  Finch says a private collector, one with a very good lawyer and a very quiet gallery.  The Archive does not involve lawyers, she adds, because lawyers require you to explain things in rooms with records.  I like that answer more than I expected to.

The door opens before she finishes, and a third kid drops into one of the empty chairs like he has been late to better things than this.  He says his name is Dash, apologizes to no one in particular, and asks whether he missed anything important.  Finch says he missed the part where she decides whether to trust any of us.  The part he is walking into now, she says, is the part where we start deciding whether to trust each other.  Nobody laughs.  I notice that the fourth chair is still empty, and that nobody else in the room has looked at it once.

passages.title: Catalog Entry: The Threadglass
passages.text:
Every object the Archive tracks gets one entry in the master catalog.  The entry is updated each time new information surfaces.  It is never deleted, even after a relic is recovered.  The entry below is the current record for catalog number 114, known informally as the Threadglass.

Description.  It is a flat disc of pale green glass, four inches across.  One face is etched with a single continuous spiral line that never crosses itself.  The etching is shallow.  It only shows clearly when light crosses the glass at an angle.  Historians believe that was done on purpose, not a flaw in the original casting.  No one has ever measured the spiral exactly the same way twice.  The line has no clear start or end for a ruler to use.

Origin.  The Threadglass turns up in written records three separate times across roughly two hundred years.  Each mention connects it to a story.  The story is about a path that could not be walked twice by accident.  Each record ties the object loosely to an older legend.  It is about a hero who escaped a builder's maze by following a single unbroken thread.  Archive researchers are careful to note something.  The disc is almost certainly a later tribute to that story, not a prop from the events the story tells.  Glassmaking this fine did not exist when the maze legend is set.

Documented history.  The disc entered the Ashford family collection in the nineteenth century.  It passed to a regional museum by gift.  It was moved twice more between institutions.  A formal count in the 1970s confirmed it was present and secure.  A second count, taken eleven years later, could not find it.  No theft was ever reported to any police record the Archive has found.  The gap between those two counts is the single largest question mark in this entry.

Current status.  Archive field work places the Threadglass in a private collection as of last spring.  The lead comes from an insurance filing.  It describes an object that matches this entry in exact size.  The filer's name is blacked out in the copy the Archive obtained.  This entry will be updated again once the object's status changes.  A note will explain how the Archive came to know it changed.

passages.title: Catalog Entry: The Wyrdstone
passages.text:
Catalog number 206 is the Archive's record for a hand-sized stone known as the Wyrdstone.  It is currently classified as missing rather than recovered.

Description.  It is a rough oval of dark grey stone.  It is cool to the touch, even in a heated room, according to three separate handling reports filed decades apart.  One face carries a cluster of carved lines in an old runic alphabet.  Specialists have only partly translated it.  The readable portion names no owner and gives no instructions.  It reads, as closely as it can be rendered, thread of what was already true.  That is not a complete sentence.  It is closer to half of one.

Origin.  Stones carved this way appear in a handful of northern legends.  The legends describe three sisters who sat beneath a great tree.  Together they carved the shape of every life as it happened, never before it happened.  Not even the sisters themselves could carve a life differently once it had begun.  The Wyrdstone is not claimed to be one of their own tools.  Archive researchers treat it as a votive object, something a believer commissioned and carved in tribute to that story.  It was most likely left at a shrine rather than carried.

Documented history.  A university excavation recovered the stone from a coastal site.  It was logged into a teaching collection, where it sat largely unexamined for over thirty years.  A visiting researcher requested it for study eight years ago.  The loan paperwork was completed and filed correctly.  The stone itself was never returned.  The researcher's listed institution has no record of anyone by that name.

Current status.  No verified sighting exists past the loan date.  The Archive lists the Wyrdstone as its oldest open case, for exactly that reason.  It was a theft with no theft report, carried out by someone who did the paperwork properly and vanished anyway.  Any lead, however small, is to be logged immediately rather than investigated alone.

passages.title: Three Realms Below
passages.text:
Every tradition the Archive studies describes a place the dead go.  Reading three of those descriptions side by side says more about how each culture explained the world than any single one does alone.

The Greek underworld is described as a single kingdom with regions inside it, the way a country has provinces.  Most of the dead are said to drift as shades through a grey plain.  They are neither rewarded nor punished, adrift in a fog most Greek writers describe as endless rather than dark.  Two smaller regions sit at the far edges of that kingdom.  One is for punishment, reserved for those who wronged the gods directly rather than other people.  One is for reward, reserved for a small number of the greatly honored.  The kingdom has a ruler, a boundary river, and a ferryman.  The ferryman will not carry a soul across without payment.  That is why the old custom of burying a coin with a body comes from this tradition specifically.

The Egyptian underworld is described less as a place than as a journey.  It is a passage through twelve regions that mirror the twelve hours of night.  Each region is guarded.  Each one requires the traveler to know the correct words to pass safely.  At the journey's end, the heart of the dead person is weighed on a scale against a single feather.  The two sides of that scale must balance exactly for the traveler to continue onward.  A heart heavier than the feather does not lead to a lesser punishment.  It ends the journey completely.  That is why so much Egyptian funeral writing is devoted to coaching the dead through this one moment, rather than describing what comes after it.

The Norse underworld splits the dead by the manner of their death, rather than by anything they did in life.  Warriors who died in battle are described as being taken to a golden hall.  There they prepare for a final conflict still to come.  Nearly everyone else travels instead to a cold and misty realm, regardless of how they lived.  That realm is ruled by a figure said to be half living and half corpse.  The dead there simply continue existing, rather than being judged.  Norse tradition spends comparatively little of its writing describing this second realm in detail.  Some Archive researchers read that gap as its own kind of statement, about which fate the culture's storytellers actually wanted to dwell on.

Read together, the three traditions disagree about almost everything.  Are the dead judged, sorted, or do they simply continue?  Does the journey matter more than the destination?  Does fairness or fate decide where anyone ends up?  On one point, though, they agree without exception.  The border between the living and the dead is a real place with real geography.  It is crossed by a real path, one the people who told these stories believed was worth describing in exact and careful detail.

passages.title: The Kade Collection
passages.text:
The card Finch gives Theo for this one has a different kind of lie built into it.  It is a laminated badge that says he is delivering a framing order to Augustine Kade's private gallery.  He also carries a flat cardboard box.  As far as Theo can tell, it contains an actual empty picture frame, in case anybody asks to see inside it.  Finch calls this kind of cover honest bait.  A delivery, she says, is the one kind of stranger a guarded building lets walk right up to the door without a second thought.

The gallery occupies the top two floors of a building with no sign on the street.  Theo has learned that is its own kind of announcement, to anyone who already knows what they are looking for.  A man at the intake desk barely looks up from his screen before waving him toward a service elevator.  Theo spends the ride up reminding himself of something.  The box in his hands is the least interesting thing he is carrying.  The interesting thing is a floor plan Mila drew from three different sets of public renovation permits, memorized rather than carried.

The gallery floor is not what Theo expected.  He pictured locked glass cases and velvet ropes, the way a museum keeps things at arm's length from visitors.  Instead the Threadglass sits on an open pedestal, in the center of a bright room, lit from above.  It is close enough to touch.  That strikes him as either supreme confidence, or a trap so obvious that nobody sane could believe it was real.  He decides it does not matter which.  His job today is not to touch anything.  His job is to look.

A woman crosses the room toward him before he has finished looking.  She moves like someone who has never once had to hurry in her life.  She introduces herself as Kade.  She says the framing order is not something she remembers placing.  Then she asks, in a tone as level as the floor, who exactly sent him.

Theo's answer is ready before he decides to give it.  The rule Finch drilled into him is simple: never invent, offer something boring that can be checked.  He says the order came through a framing shop two streets over.  He gives the shop's real name.  He offers to leave the frame and come back, once she has sorted out the confusion on her end.  It is a true detail wrapped around a lie.  True details are the only kind that survive a phone call.

Kade studies him for exactly as long as it takes to decide he is not worth the effort of catching in something.  Then she tells him to leave the box at the desk on his way out.  Theo does exactly that.  He does not look at the pedestal again on his way past it.  He has already counted the four exits and the two visible cameras.  He has already noticed that the pedestal has no case around it at all, only a thin dark line in the floor circling it, like a fence nobody could see unless they already knew where to look.

passages.title: Two Exits, One Elevator
passages.text:
My job today is to sit on a bench across the street from a building with no sign on it, counting how many times the revolving door spins.  Finch calls this reconnaissance.  I call it the longest forty minutes of my life.  I would never say that on the radio, though, because Mila is listening on the other channel, and she has strong opinions about people who complain on an open line.

Theo went in at eleven on the dot, carrying a box I know for a fact holds nothing but an empty picture frame.  That is either the cleverest cover story I have ever heard, or the kind of thing that only works because nobody expects it to be that simple.  The plan says he checks in by eleven-fifteen.  I have a radio, a folded map of the block, and a sandwich I am too nervous to eat.

At eleven-eleven a delivery van double-parks in front of the building, blocking my clean view of the door for almost two full minutes.  That is exactly the kind of detail nobody plans for, and everybody should.  I write the time down anyway, because Finch's rule is simple: log what you saw, not what you decided it meant.  I did not see Theo during those two minutes.  That is a fact.  It is not the same fact as something has gone wrong.

The van pulls away at eleven-thirteen, and the door is exactly as empty as it was before it arrived.  That could mean nothing happened in the two minutes I could not see.  It could also mean something happened fast enough to be finished by the time the van cleared.  I do not love that second possibility, so I decide not to keep thinking about it, and count the door again instead.

At eleven-fourteen the revolving door spits Theo out onto the sidewalk, without the box.  He walks at exactly the speed of someone who is not in a hurry.  That, I have learned by now, is the only speed that ever looks right from a distance.  He does not look at my bench.  I do not wave.  We are, by design, two strangers who have never met, walking away from the same building in two different directions.  It will be four more blocks before either of us is allowed to admit otherwise.

I key the radio twice, which means clear, no pickup.  I get one click back, which means received.  I fold my map and leave half the sandwich for whichever pigeon has been watching me watch the door.  Whatever those two minutes behind the van turn out to have cost us, I think, at least I wrote the time down honestly, before I knew whether it mattered.

passages.title: Three Seconds
passages.text:
Finch reads debrief logs out loud.  Nobody warned Theo about that beforehand.  He now understands it is deliberate, the same way she never explains a test until it is already halfway finished.

Dash's log is thorough to the point of stubbornness.  It gives the exact minute the van double-parked, and the exact minute it left.  It states flatly that the door was empty both before and after, and that nothing could be confirmed about the two minutes in between.  Finch reads that last line twice.  Most people, she says, watching a door for forty minutes, would have quietly decided what probably happened during a gap they could not see.  They would have written down the decision instead of the gap.  Dash wrote down the gap.

Theo's log says he entered, spoke with a woman who introduced herself as Kade, delivered a cover story about a framing order, and left without incident.  It is a true and complete account of everything Theo did.  Finch asks him a single question that was not in his log at all.  What changed about Kade's face, in the three seconds after he mentioned the name of the framing shop?  Theo starts to say nothing.  Then he catches himself.  He admits that something had changed, something small around her eyes, that he noticed and immediately decided was not important enough to write down.

Finch says that is precisely the kind of detail the whole exercise exists to catch.  A person's claim about what happened, and the full truth of what happened, are not automatically the same size.  Theo's claim, I entered and left without incident, is completely accurate.  It still leaves out the one moment that might matter most: a flicker of recognition on Kade's face, at the mention of a shop two streets over.  That flicker either means nothing at all, or it means Kade already knew that shop's name before Theo ever said it.

Nobody in the room can tell yet which of those two explanations is true.  Not knowing yet is fine, Finch says, and is in fact the honest answer.  But only if the detail gets written down where somebody can weigh it later, rather than quietly decided and dropped, the way Theo nearly dropped it.  She hands the log back to him with one instruction.  Add the missing three seconds, exactly as he saw them, with no guess attached about what they meant.  Theo writes for longer than three seconds took to happen, choosing each word the way he wishes he had chosen his first version.

passages.title: Source A: The Temple Chronicle
passages.text:
The text below is a translation of an inscription, carved into the inner wall of a temple chamber at Abydos.  Temple scribes of this period wrote to honor the priesthood that commissioned their work.  This chronicle carries no author's name, only the seal of the temple itself.

The god Osiris was struck down by his brother Set.  His body was scattered beyond the borders of the living world.  It was Isis who would not accept the loss as final.  She searched every province of the kingdom herself, refusing all rest.  She gathered every piece of what Set had scattered.  An ordinary mourner would have wept.  Isis worked instead.  An ordinary sister would have given up the search after the first province turned up nothing.  Isis pressed on, through all the provinces that remained.

Isis restored her brother enough to grant him a final breath of life.  Still, she knew something.  Set's jealousy would not rest simply because Osiris had been mourned properly.  She carried a single seal, cut from the same stone as the temple's own base.  She pressed it into the innermost room of this very temple.  Sealed within it was a piece of what she had restored, so that Set's followers could never undo it.

The seal remains in this chamber to this day.  It is protected by the priesthood that has kept this temple since the reign of the chronicle's own commissioning king, and by his line after him, without interruption.  No enemy of the temple has ever set foot in this chamber.  The chronicle exists to record that fact, for every generation of priests who serve here after the scribes who carved it have themselves passed into the west.

Let it be known, to any who read this wall, that the temple's protection over the seal is not a claim requiring proof.  It is a fact requiring only faith.  It is maintained by the priesthood the gods themselves selected for this single purpose, generation after generation, without a single failure the temple's own records have ever needed to explain.

passages.title: Source B: The Reckoner's Ledger
passages.text:
The text below is a page from a ledger, kept by a guild of tomb entrants who operated across several centuries.  It was passed down and added to by each generation of the guild, rather than written by a single hand.  This page is written in the first person, by an entrant identified only by the guild rank of Reckoner.  That title was given to whoever had most recently proven a chronicle wrong.

Every temple claims its innermost chamber has never been entered.  Every temple is wrong at least once.  I know this because I am writing from inside the very chamber the Abydos priests have sworn, for six generations, that no enemy has ever reached.

The chronicle on their wall says Isis sealed a piece of Osiris's restoration here, cut from the temple's own foundation stone.  I found the seal exactly where the wall says it should be.  It is real.  It is exactly as old as the priests believe.  The wall does not say something, though, because the priests who carved it did not know it themselves.  The seal had already been moved once before I arrived, generations earlier, by an entrant whose name our guild no longer records.  It was quietly returned to this same chamber, by a hand that was never caught.  I know this because the setting stone beneath the seal shows two different tool marks, from two different centuries.  A priest trained only to guard, never to examine, would never have thought to look.

I am not removing the seal.  A guild that removes what it finds is a guild that gets hunted.  A guild that gets hunted stops finding anything at all.  I am recording what the wall got wrong, for the next Reckoner.  I am leaving the seal precisely as I found it, tool marks and all.  The temple's faith remains exactly as undisturbed as their chronicle claims it to be.

Let the next entrant know this.  The true history of this chamber is not the one carved on its wall.  It is not the one our own guild likes to tell about itself, either.  It is only ever the one written down by whoever last stood here, and looked closely enough to see both.

passages.title: What the Archive Believes
passages.text:
Two accounts of the Abydos seal chamber survive in Archive records.  They agree with each other far less than a reader might expect, from two sources describing the same small room.

The temple chronicle was carved by scribes working for the priesthood itself.  It claims the chamber has never been entered by anyone the temple did not choose.  Claims like this one are hard to weigh on their own terms.  The same group that guards the chamber is also the group writing its history.  A guard has an obvious reason to report a perfect record.  That is true whether or not the record is actually perfect.  That does not make the chronicle false.  It makes the chronicle a source that cannot check itself, which is a different problem, and a more common one.

The guild ledger tells a very different story.  It claims the chamber was entered.  Physical evidence proves it, the ledger says: two sets of tool marks on the setting stone, left by two different people across two different centuries.  A claim resting on physical evidence is generally easier to weigh than a claim resting on faith.  Tool marks either exist or they do not, and a later examiner could in principle check them.  The ledger's weak point runs the other way.  It survives only in a guild's own private record, kept by people whose trade depended on nobody outside the guild ever reading it.  A private record kept by thieves carries its own reason to stretch the truth, to tell a story that makes the guild look skilled and careful rather than reckless.

Archive researchers do not assign weight to either account simply because it sounds more convincing.  The chronicle's claim is unverifiable by its very nature.  No outside party was ever allowed to check it.  The ledger's claim is, in principle, verifiable.  Tool marks either are or are not present on that stone.  But nobody outside the guild has ever been permitted to look.  Until an Archive researcher can examine the setting stone directly, the honest record is not that one source is right and the other wrong.  It is that one source has told a story nobody could ever check.  The other has told a story that could be checked, and simply never was.

That is why this entry, unlike most in the catalog, ends without a conclusion.  The seal's history is not settled.  It is only better understood.

passages.title: The Frostbank Vault
passages.text:
Frostbank Storage keeps its lowest floor at a temperature the brochure calls archival.  Mila calls it simply cold.  It is the kind of cold that finds the gap between a coat's top button and a scarf within the first ten seconds, and settles there like it has been invited.  She has been inside four minutes.  She has already stopped noticing the cold as cold, and started noticing it as a sound: a low mechanical hum, filling the corridor the way silence fills a held breath.

Her cover today is thinner than Theo's ever get: a badge borrowed from a records-transfer service.  It is good for exactly one door, before someone checks a list she is not on.  She has counted eleven doors already.  The twelfth is the one that matters.  It sits at the end of a corridor so featureless that the ceiling lights seem to recede toward it, like the narrowing end of a tunnel.  Each light is slightly dimmer than the last.  Mila genuinely cannot decide whether that is by design, or a trick of the cold.

The vault door itself is unremarkable: a slab of pale metal, with a single reader panel.  Mila finds that disappointing, in a way she was not expecting.  A room this deliberately built to feel like the edge of the world, she thinks, owed her something more dramatic at the actual edge.  The badge reads green.  The door releases with a sound less like an opening and more like something exhaling, a long low breath of air that had clearly been sealed in for longer than eleven minutes could explain.

Inside, the Wyrdstone sits alone on a raised shelf, under a single cone of light.  The rest of the room falls away into a darkness so complete that Mila cannot see the far wall.  She can only sense it, the way you sense a person standing just behind you before you turn around.  The stone itself looks smaller than the catalog photograph suggested, almost disappointingly plain, a grey oval that could be mistaken for nothing more than a stone someone picked up on a beach and never put down.  She does not touch it.  Her job today is only to confirm it is here.  She notes, for whoever comes back to actually take it, that the room's only camera sits directly above the shelf.  It points straight down, blind to everything but the four square feet it was built to watch.

Walking back out through the twelve doors, Mila counts them again in reverse.  She notices, for the first time, that the corridor felt longer walking in than it does walking out.  A held breath always feels longer than the exhale that finally lets it go.

passages.title: No Hurry At All
passages.text:
I have never been so aware of my own breathing as I am right now, sitting in a rented car outside a building with the word Frostbank stamped across it, in letters too small for a place that size, watching a door that has not moved in eleven minutes.

Mila went in at two, and she checks in by two-twenty.  If the radio stays silent past two-twenty-five, the plan says I call Finch, and the whole thing ends, whatever ends turns out to mean for someone still inside.  I have read that rule so many times in my head that it has stopped sounding like words.  Now it sounds like a countdown.

The building itself does not help.  It is the kind of gray that is not really a color, so much as an absence of one, low and flat, built without a single window on this side.  From where I sit, it looks less like a place people work and more like something that grew out of the parking lot on its own, patient, in no hurry, the way glaciers are in no hurry.  I decide that comparison is not helping either, and try to stop making them.

At two-nineteen a service van pulls up to a loading door I did not know existed, blocking most of my view of the entrance Mila actually used.  My whole chest does something unpleasant and sudden, a cold drop like a missed stair in the dark.  I remind myself, out loud, quietly, that a service van is the single most ordinary thing that could possibly happen outside a storage building on a weekday afternoon.  My chest does not currently have access to that information.  It is reacting anyway.

The van pulls away at two-twenty-two, though the door is still closed.  I have three minutes left on the plan's own clock, and I spend every second of them doing the thing Finch actually trained into me: naming what I know, instead of guessing what I fear.  Mila went in at two.  The badge she carries is good.  Nothing on this street has made a sound that means trouble.  Fear is not evidence, no matter how loudly it argues that it is.

At two-twenty-four the radio clicks twice, and I let out a breath I did not know I had been holding for four straight minutes.  I write the real time down next to the time the plan expected.  Finch always asks for both.  A plan that is only ever right on paper, she says, is not actually a plan you can trust.

passages.title: The Weight of a Thread
passages.text:
Finch tells the story the same way every time.  The crew has learned that means it matters to her.  Everything she does not care about, she tells a different way each time, just to see who is actually listening.

There were three sisters, she says, who sat beneath the oldest tree anyone had a name for.  Between them, they carved the shape of every life exactly as it happened.  Not before it happened.  Exactly as it happened, stroke by stroke, so close behind the living that no one, not even the sisters, could say for certain whether the carving caused the moment, or the moment caused the carving.  People who wanted to know their own future used to travel to that tree.  They would beg the sisters to carve ahead, just once, just a little.  The sisters never did.  Not from cruelty, Finch says.  Carving ahead was the one thing even they did not know how to do safely.  The three of them had long ago agreed that safety mattered more than anyone's curiosity, including their own.

She lets that sit for a moment before she tells the crew why she is telling it.  A field report, she says, is exactly that kind of carving.  It has to be cut stroke by stroke behind the moment, never ahead of it.  It records only what happened, not what somebody standing there expected to happen, or hoped would happen next.  A report that carves ahead of the truth, even a little, even with the best intentions in the world, stops being a record.  It starts being a guess wearing a record's clothing.  Nobody down the line can tell the difference just by looking at it.

Dash asks whether the sisters ever got it wrong.  Finch says that is the wrong question.  The right one is whether anybody ever caught them at it.  The two are not the same thing, she says, and mixing them up is exactly the mistake the story exists to prevent.  She taps the stone sitting in its case at the center of the table: the Wyrdstone, cool even through the glass.  It was carved by someone who believed the story enough to spend months carving a tribute to it.  Whatever else the crew decides about the sisters, she says, the person who made this stone believed one thing.  The difference between wrong and uncaught mattered enough to spend a season of their life saying so in rock.

passages.title: The Vault of Ages
passages.text:
Finch told us on the first day that the Archive goes deeper than the last hundred people who walked past it ever guessed.  I spent months assuming that was the kind of thing trainers say to sound impressive.  Now I am standing at the bottom of a staircase that should not exist, under a library that closed two winters ago.  I am looking at a door with no handle and no keyhole, only a spiral etched into its center.  It matches the pattern on a piece of glass I once delivered in a picture-frame box.  I am revising that assumption completely.

Kade found this door before we did.  That is the only reason any of us are standing here at eleven at night, instead of asleep in our own beds.  Three relics were taken, from three different collections, over three different decades.  Finch says every one of them was never really the target.  Each one was a key, cut to fit a different notch in a lock built to need all three at once.  Kade spent years collecting keys, without ever telling herself, or anyone else, what door they were for.  We only worked that out because Mila noticed the same spiral, scaled three different ways, on three objects that supposedly had nothing to do with each other.

Dash sets the Wyrdstone into the leftmost notch first.  Dash always wants to be the one who finds out what happens next.  For one long second, nothing happens at all.  That is somehow worse than something happening badly would have been.  Then the spiral on the door catches a thread of light, from somewhere inside it that was clearly never powered by anything as ordinary as electricity.  I stop breathing, the way I stopped breathing outside Frostbank.  Except this time there is no radio to click twice and tell me it is fine.

Mila sets the seal into the center notch.  She reads the tool marks on its underside one more time, like she is checking a signature.  It is the same care she has given every piece of evidence, since the day she counted two empty chairs and decided the question that actually mattered was the one nobody had answered yet.  I set the Threadglass last, into the notch on the right.  The whole door goes quiet, in a way that is somehow louder than the sound it was making a second ago.

The door does not open like a door.  It opens like a held breath finally let go.  What is on the other side is not gold, or gods, or anything a story would have promised us.  It is shelves, ordinary as any library's, holding centuries of objects that people once loved enough to hide.  Kade is not standing among them.  It turns out Kade spent years finding the keys and never noticed the three of us slip past her, at the door she thought she alone knew how to open.  Finch always said noticing was the only qualification that ever mattered here.  I am standing in a room that should not exist, holding nothing but a working radio and the exact right kind of luck.  I finally understand that she meant it as a warning as much as a compliment.

partA.stem: Why does Theo almost throw the card away?
choices: A stranger who knew something he never said out loud is an unsettling thought at night.
He does not think the card was meant for him.
He suspects a classmate from school sent it as a joke.
He dislikes getting mail after nine o'clock.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: It is plain white and unlined, and it holds exactly six words in handwriting so neat it looks printed: You noticed the gap.
The card slides under Theo Brack's door at eleven at night, which is already strange, since nobody in this building visits after nine.
He almost throws the card away, because a stranger who knows what you noticed and never said out loud is not a comforting thought at eleven at night.
Nobody else on this floor has ever mentioned it.

distractorRationale.1: The neat handwriting is a detail about how the note looks, not about who it is for. Nothing in the passage suggests Theo doubts the card was addressed to him.
distractorRationale.2: Nobody else mentioning the floorboard tells you Theo has kept the detail to himself. It does not point to a classmate or a joke, and the passage never mentions school at all.
distractorRationale.3: The nine o'clock detail explains why the timing feels strange, not why Theo almost throws the card away. He is unsettled by what the card knows, not by when it arrived.

items.explain: Theo almost throws the card away because it proves someone else has been watching closely enough to notice something he never told anyone. That is unsettling on its own, independent of the hour or the handwriting.

partA.stem: What does Theo notice about the Athenaeum before he goes inside?
choices: The front doors are chained shut, but a side door stands open a crack.
The building has a new sign advertising its reopening.
Lights are burning in every window.
A guard is posted at the front entrance.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: Theo has walked past its boarded windows a hundred times without once wondering what was still inside.
The Athenaeum's front doors are chained, exactly as they have been for two years.
A side door under the fire escape stands open half an inch, as if somebody left it that way on purpose, confident nobody else would ever try it.
Inside, the dust is thinner than it should be for a building that has been empty two years, which means somebody has been walking these floors more recently than the chained doors suggest.

distractorRationale.1: The passage says the building has sat dark since it closed two winters ago. Walking past its boarded windows a hundred times is not the same as a sign announcing it will reopen.
distractorRationale.2: The passage never describes the windows as lit. The line about dust tells you the inside is mostly undisturbed, which argues against anyone leaving lights burning.
distractorRationale.3: The chained front doors are the only security the passage describes. Nothing in the text mentions a guard, and a chain is what a building uses instead of one.

items.explain: The chained front doors look secure, but the side door standing open half an inch is the detail that actually matters. It is the one gap in an otherwise locked building, exactly the kind of small inconsistency the story trains Theo, and the reader, to notice.

partA.stem: The story is told from outside Theo's head, in the third person, but it still lets readers know what he is privately thinking. Which detail best shows this?
choices: The narration says walking through the gap is "the first real decision he has made in longer than he wants to admit."
The narration describes the card as plain white and unlined.
The narration explains that the Athenaeum closed two winters ago.
The narration notes that Finch is standing with her arms folded.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: A woman is waiting at the bottom of a spiral staircase, arms folded, watching him arrive with an expression that is not quite a smile.
It is also the first real decision he has made in longer than he wants to admit.
It closed to the public two winters ago and has sat dark ever since.
It is plain white and unlined, and it holds exactly six words in handwriting so neat it looks printed: You noticed the gap.

distractorRationale.1: This line describes what the card physically looks like. It tells you nothing about what Theo is thinking or feeling as he reads it.
distractorRationale.2: This is a plain fact about the building's history. A narrator could report it without any access to a character's private thoughts at all.
distractorRationale.3: Folded arms and a not-quite-smile describe Finch from the outside, the way a stranger watching the scene might describe her. It says nothing about Theo's inner thoughts.

items.explain: A narrator writing from outside a character's head can still reveal that character's private thoughts through word choice, not just physical description. Calling the decision one Theo "wants to admit" is a judgment only someone with access to his private thinking could report.

partA.stem: What does Finch actually test Theo on during their first conversation?
choices: Small details he noticed on his way into the building.
How well he can pick a lock.
How fast he can run up a staircase.
Whether he can keep a secret from his family.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: A side door under the fire escape stands open half an inch, as if somebody left it that way on purpose, confident nobody else would ever try it.
Nobody else on this floor has ever mentioned it.
She asks about the chain that was not actually locked, the light under the door that nobody left on by accident, and the exact spot where the newer dust ended and the older dust began.
Then she turns and starts down a second staircase, one Theo did not know was there, and does not look back to see if he is following, because by then she already knows he is.

distractorRationale.1: The open side door is a detail Theo notices, not a lock Finch asks him to pick. The passage never describes any lock-picking at all.
distractorRationale.2: The second staircase appears at the very end of the scene, after the questioning is already finished. It has nothing to do with speed or running.
distractorRationale.3: This line is about the floorboard, not about family or secrecy. The passage never mentions Theo's family.

items.explain: Finch's questions are all about small, easy-to-miss details from Theo's walk in: an unlocked chain, a light left on, where the dust changes. That pattern of questions is the actual test, not anything physical like running or picking locks.

items.stem: Choose the three details that show the Athenaeum is not really as empty as it looks from the street.
choices: The dust inside is thinner than it should be for a building empty two years.
A side door under the fire escape stands open half an inch.
The front doors are chained shut.
A woman is waiting at the bottom of a staircase inside.
The windows are boarded up.
The building closed to the public two winters ago.

distractorRationale.2: Chained doors are exactly what an abandoned building is supposed to look like. This detail supports the idea that the building is empty, not the opposite.
distractorRationale.4: Boarded windows are ordinary for a closed building. They do not suggest anyone is still using the space inside.
distractorRationale.5: The closing date explains why the building looks empty. It does not tell you anything about what is happening inside it right now.

items.explain: Three details work against the building's abandoned appearance: the dust is too thin, a side door is left open on purpose, and someone is actually waiting inside. Chained doors, boarded windows, and the closing date are exactly what an empty building should look like, so they do not count as evidence against it.

partA.stem: What happened to the Threadglass?
choices: It was documented in three archives, then vanished from all of them within the same decade.
It was destroyed in a fire at a museum.
It was donated to the Archive by its original owner.
It has never been seen by anyone outside Finch's crew.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: Finch says a private collector, one with a very good lawyer and a very quiet gallery.
Someone wanted it enough to risk being caught holding it, three times, in three different countries.
Then it vanished from all three collections within the same decade.
She tells us the disc in the photograph has a name, the Threadglass, documented in three separate archives across two centuries.

distractorRationale.1: Being risky to hold is not the same as being destroyed. The passage describes the Threadglass being taken and hidden, and never mentions a fire.
distractorRationale.2: A private collector holding the disc is the opposite of a donation. The passage never says who originally gave it to anyone.
distractorRationale.3: Being documented in three separate archives across two centuries is the opposite of never being seen. Plenty of people saw it before it disappeared.

items.explain: The Threadglass has a public paper trail: three archives recorded it over two centuries. Then, within one decade, it vanished from all three collections at once, which is the detail this item is asking about directly.

partA.stem: Mila tells this story in the first person. Which detail best shows what kind of person she is, through what she notices first?
choices: She notices the two empty chairs before Finch has said a single word.
She notices that Theo seems nervous talking to a stranger.
She notices that the photograph shows a glass disc.
She notices that a private collector now owns the Threadglass.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: She sets a single photograph on the table between us: a glass disc, roughly the size of a coaster, etched with a pattern that curves in on itself like a shell.
I count four chairs around Finch's table, and only two of them get used, which tells me something before anyone says a word.
Finch says a private collector, one with a very good lawyer and a very quiet gallery.
He introduces himself as Theo, then seems to regret it immediately, like talking to a stranger is a skill he is still building.

distractorRationale.1: Noticing Theo's nervousness says something about Theo. It does not show what Mila herself pays attention to first, before anyone has even spoken.
distractorRationale.2: The photograph is a detail about what Finch shows the group, not a choice Mila made about what to notice on her own.
distractorRationale.3: This is information about who owns the Threadglass now. It is a plot detail, not a moment that reveals anything about Mila's own habits of attention.

items.explain: Mila counts the chairs and clocks the empty ones before Finch has said a single word, which shows a habit of noticing gaps and absences first. That instinct, introduced in the very first line, turns out to define her voice for the rest of the passage.

partA.stem: Why does Finch say the Archive does not involve lawyers?
choices: Because lawyers require explaining things in rooms with records.
Because the Archive cannot afford legal fees.
Because Kade already has a lawyer working against them.
Because lawyers are not allowed inside the Athenaeum.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: I have known her for eleven minutes, and I already understand that this is going to be a pattern.
She wants to know if we want it back badly enough to take a much smaller risk than that.
Finch says a private collector, one with a very good lawyer and a very quiet gallery.
The Archive does not involve lawyers, she adds, because lawyers require you to explain things in rooms with records.

distractorRationale.1: This line describes the collector's lawyer, the person the Archive is up against. It says nothing about whether the Archive itself can afford one.
distractorRationale.2: This line is about how Finch answers questions in general. It has nothing to do with lawyers or legal risk specifically.
distractorRationale.3: The risk Finch mentions is about taking the Threadglass back, not about a rule against lawyers entering any particular building.

items.explain: Finch gives one exact reason for skipping lawyers: they need explanations that end up in official records. That reason is about avoiding a paper trail, not about cost, location, or Kade's own legal team.

partA.stem: What happens right as Finch is about to finish explaining the mission?
choices: A third kid, Dash, arrives late and drops into one of the empty chairs.
Finch reveals who currently owns the Threadglass.
The photograph of the Threadglass disappears from the table.
Theo decides he does not want to help find the Threadglass.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: She sets a single photograph on the table between us: a glass disc, roughly the size of a coaster, etched with a pattern that curves in on itself like a shell.
The door opens before she finishes, and a third kid drops into one of the empty chairs like he has been late to better things than this.
I decide I like him better for that than I would have liked someone smooth.
Finch says a private collector, one with a very good lawyer and a very quiet gallery.

distractorRationale.1: Finch does explain who owns the Threadglass, but that happens earlier in the conversation, well before the door opens at the end of the scene.
distractorRationale.2: The photograph is placed on the table near the start of the scene. Nothing in the passage says it disappears at any point.
distractorRationale.3: This line is Mila's private opinion about Theo. It never suggests Theo wants to back out of the mission.

items.explain: The door interrupts Finch mid-sentence, right as she is wrapping up, and Dash drops into one of the two empty chairs everyone has been quietly wondering about. That timing, right at the end of the scene, is what this item is asking about.

items.stem: Choose the three details that reveal something about how Finch runs a meeting, rather than a fact about the Threadglass itself.
choices: She sets a photograph on the table instead of explaining out loud first.
She answers "that is the correct question" without actually answering it.
The Threadglass was documented in three separate archives.
She lets Dash's late arrival pass without much comment, and turns it into a lesson instead.
A private collector currently owns the Threadglass.
The disc is etched with a spiral pattern.

distractorRationale.2: This is a fact about the Threadglass's history. It does not describe anything Finch does or says in the scene.
distractorRationale.4: This is a fact about who owns the object right now. It is plot information, not a detail about how Finch runs the meeting.
distractorRationale.5: This describes the object's appearance. It has nothing to do with Finch's own behavior or personality.

items.explain: Finch reveals her personality through method rather than explanation: she shows instead of tells, praises a good question without giving away the answer, and turns Dash's lateness into a teaching moment on the spot. Facts about the Threadglass itself do not show anything about Finch.

items.stem: Tap the three sentences that show Finch testing Theo through small questions rather than asking him outright why he came.
spans: Finch does not ask why he came.
She asks what he noticed on the way in, then keeps asking, question after small question.
She asks about the chain that was not actually locked, the light under the door that nobody left on by accident, and the exact spot where the newer dust ended and the older dust began.
Theo answers every one, and only once he stops talking does he realize that he has been tested for twenty minutes and never once felt like he was being tested.
Finch tells him that noticing is the only qualification that has ever mattered here, and that the building goes a great deal deeper than the last hundred people who walked past it ever guessed.
items.explain: The three chosen sentences describe what Finch actually does: she skips the direct question and instead narrows in on small details, the chain, the light, the dust. If you picked Theo's realization or Finch's closing lesson, you flagged the effect of her method or her verdict afterward, not the questioning itself.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences where Mila shares a private judgment that only her first-person narration could reveal. The other two simply report what someone said aloud.
spans: I have known her for eleven minutes, and I already understand that this is going to be a pattern.
I like that answer more than I expected to.
Finch says a private collector, one with a very good lawyer and a very quiet gallery.
He says his name is Dash, apologizes to no one in particular, and asks whether he missed anything important.
items.explain: Both chosen lines step outside plain reporting into Mila's own head, a pattern she has decided she is noticing and a reaction she did not expect to have. If you picked either quoted line of dialogue instead, you mistook something someone else said aloud for a judgment only Mila's own narration could supply.

items.stem: Tap the three phrases that describe the note itself. The other two describe the hallway detail the note is about.
spans: plain white and unlined
exactly six words in handwriting so neat it looks printed
You noticed the gap.
the loose floorboard in the third-floor hallway
stepping on it makes a sound like a complaint
items.explain: All three chosen phrases describe the note itself, its plain appearance, its neat handwriting, and its six-word message. The floorboard and the sound it makes describe the hallway detail the note refers to, not the note. Ask which noun a phrase is actually describing before you tap it.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences where the narrator uses a because clause to explain a character's unspoken feeling. The other two state a plain fact with no inner state attached.
spans: Then she turns and starts down a second staircase, one Theo did not know was there, and does not look back to see if he is following, because by then she already knows he is.
He almost throws the card away, because a stranger who knows what you noticed and never said out loud is not a comforting thought at eleven at night.
Finch tells him that noticing is the only qualification that has ever mattered here, and that the building goes a great deal deeper than the last hundred people who walked past it ever guessed.
The Athenaeum's front doors are chained, exactly as they have been for two years.
items.explain: Both chosen sentences use a because clause to let the narrator explain a character's unspoken certainty or unease, Finch's confidence that Theo is following and Theo's own discomfort with the card. The lesson about noticing is something Finch actually says out loud, and the chained doors are a plain fact with no inner state attached at all.

items.stem: Finish the summary. Theo almost throws the note away because {{0}}, but the next day he goes to the Athenaeum anyway because {{1}}.

choices: a stranger who noticed something he never told anyone is unsettling to think about
the handwriting looks messy and hard to read
he does not believe the note is meant for him
sitting at home wondering about it feels worse than whatever he might find out
a second note arrives telling him to hurry
his family insists he go find out who sent it

items.explain: The note unsettles Theo because it proves someone else noticed a secret he never spoke aloud, and what finally moves him is not new information but the plain fact that not knowing has become worse than any answer could be. A second note and a nagging family are both invented; neither appears anywhere in the passage.

items.stem: Complete the summary of how Mila's narration works. Because Mila tells the story in the first person, readers learn {{0}}, and her opening line about counting chairs shows readers {{1}} before Finch has said anything at all.

choices: her own private thoughts and reactions, not just what everyone in the room can see
exactly what Theo and Dash are privately thinking too
only the events a hidden camera would record
that she notices absences and gaps before anyone explains them
that she is afraid of Finch
that she already knows about the Threadglass

items.explain: First-person narration limits the story to what happens inside one head, Mila's, which is why readers know her private reactions but never Theo's or Dash's. Her very first sentence, about counting chairs, establishes her defining habit immediately: noticing a gap before anyone has explained it, a pattern the rest of the passage keeps confirming.

items.stem: Why has Theo stepped over the loose floorboard every day for the past year, instead of just walking on it?
choices: Stepping on it makes a sound like a complaint, and nobody on the floor has ever mentioned it.
His landlord warned him never to step on that spot.
He does not realize the floorboard is loose.
The floorboard is sharp enough to be dangerous.

distractorRationale.1: The passage never mentions a landlord or any warning about the floorboard. You are adding a detail the text does not actually give you.
distractorRationale.2: The note itself proves Theo already knows about the gap, and he has stepped over it deliberately every day for a year. If you picked this, you missed that the whole point of the note is that he noticed it.
distractorRationale.3: Nothing in the passage describes the floorboard as sharp or dangerous, only loud. You may be assuming a reason that sounds plausible instead of reading what the text actually says.

items.explain: The passage states the reason directly: stepping on the floorboard makes a sound like a complaint, and Theo has quietly avoided it for a year without either of them ever bringing it up. That small, private habit is exactly the kind of detail the story trains readers to notice.

items.stem: Before the card slides under his door, how does Theo generally think about the Athenaeum?
choices: He often imagined the building was haunted.
He has walked past its boarded windows a hundred times without once wondering what was still inside.
He always suspected something valuable was hidden there.
He avoided walking anywhere near the building.

distractorRationale.0: The passage never mentions Theo thinking the building was haunted. You are inventing a feeling the text does not describe.
distractorRationale.2: The whole point of this detail is that Theo suspected nothing at all before the card arrived. If you picked this, you reversed the passage's actual meaning.
distractorRationale.3: Walking past the windows a hundred times is the opposite of avoiding the building. You may have skipped over the word "past."

items.explain: The passage is specific that Theo passed the Athenaeum constantly without any curiosity at all, which makes the card's arrival a real turning point rather than the confirmation of something he already suspected.

items.stem: Why does Mila choose the chair nearest the door?
choices: It is the only chair left by the time she arrives.
Finch specifically assigns her that seat.
She says she likes knowing where the door is, a small preference that hints at a cautious personality.
It is closest to the photograph Finch sets on the table.

distractorRationale.0: Mila arrives early enough to have a choice; the passage never suggests other chairs are already taken when she sits down. You may be assuming a reason that fits a different kind of scene.
distractorRationale.1: Nobody assigns seats in this scene. Mila makes her own choice, and her own narration tells you exactly why.
distractorRationale.3: The photograph is not placed on the table until after everyone is already seated. If you picked this, you reordered events that happen in the opposite sequence.

items.explain: Mila explains her own reasoning directly, in her own first-person voice: she likes knowing where the door is. That small, deliberate choice is exactly the kind of detail only first-person narration can hand a reader so plainly.

items.stem: According to Finch, what changes once Dash joins Theo and Mila at the table?
choices: Finch decides she can no longer trust any of the three.
The group must now vote on every future decision.
Dash is immediately given final say over the mission.
The question shifts from whether Finch trusts them to whether the three of them can trust each other.

distractorRationale.0: Finch's words describe a shift, not a loss of trust on her part. If you picked this, you read her comment as more negative than the passage actually states.
distractorRationale.1: Voting is never mentioned anywhere in this scene. You may be filling in a detail the text never gives you.
distractorRationale.2: Nothing in the passage puts Dash in charge of anything. He arrives late and is treated the same as Theo and Mila, not given special authority.

items.explain: Finch draws a clear line: the part about whether she trusts them is finishing, and a new part is beginning, whether the three of them can trust each other. That shift matters because it points the story toward the crew's relationships, not just their relationship with Finch.

items.stem: Finch says the Threadglass was taken from three different countries. What does this detail suggest about whoever wanted it?
choices: Someone valued it enough to risk being caught multiple times, in multiple places.
No single collector ever cared enough to keep it safely.
The object was too fragile to stay anywhere for long.
Museums kept accidentally losing track of the same object.

distractorRationale.1: Being taken three times is evidence of strong interest, not a lack of care. You may have reversed what repeated risk-taking actually shows about the collector.
distractorRationale.2: Fragility is never mentioned anywhere in this passage. You are supplying an explanation the text does not offer.
distractorRationale.3: Finch's word choice, that someone "risked being caught," describes a deliberate act, not an accident. If you picked this, you turned an intentional theft into carelessness.

items.explain: Finch's own phrasing makes the point directly: someone was willing to risk getting caught three separate times, in three separate countries, which shows real, sustained determination rather than an accident or a lack of interest from anyone involved.

items.stem: When Theo says the etched pattern looks like "a maze with no walls," how does Mila react, in her own narration?
choices: She tells Theo his answer is wrong.
She admits it is a better answer than her own would have been, since she was still counting the empty chairs.
She ignores his answer completely and changes the subject.
She repeats his answer back to Finch as if it were her own idea.

distractorRationale.0: Mila never says Theo's answer is wrong. She actually admits it is better than what she would have offered, which is closer to the opposite of this choice.
distractorRationale.2: Mila's narration responds directly to Theo's answer instead of moving past it. If you picked this, you skipped the sentence where she reacts to what he said.
distractorRationale.3: Nothing in the passage shows Mila claiming Theo's idea as her own. Her narration credits the comparison to him, not to herself.

items.explain: Mila's first-person narration lets readers see a private, generous admission that only her own point of view could reveal: Theo's answer beats the one she would have given, because she was too busy counting chairs to notice the pattern herself.

items.stem: Match each detail Theo notices about the Athenaeum to what it actually reveals.
rowLabels: Dust noticeably thinner than two years of neglect should leave behind
A side door standing open half an inch under the fire escape
The exact line where the newer dust ends and the older dust begins
colLabels: Someone left it that way on purpose, expecting Theo specifically to use it
Marks about when a new, specific path through the building started being used
Shows the building has had far more foot traffic than a sealed building should
items.explain: Each clue points to a different kind of activity: the overall thinness of the dust shows general recent use, the open door shows a deliberate invitation rather than an accident, and the sharp boundary between old and new dust marks when one specific new path started being walked. Treating all three clues as saying the same thing blurs three separate observations into one vague idea.

items.stem: Match each crew member to their first action in this scene.
colLabels: Arrives late, drops into a chair, and apologizes to no one in particular
Takes a seat without asking if it is taken, then instantly regrets giving his name
Chooses the seat nearest the door on purpose, to know where the exit is
items.explain: Each character's very first action works like a small introduction: Theo's instant regret at oversharing, Dash's breezy apology to a room he just interrupted, and Mila's deliberate choice of the seat nearest the door. Mixing up which action belongs to which character loses exactly the kind of detail first-person narration is built to deliver.

partA.stem: This entry is organized into four labeled sections. What is the purpose of the "Documented history" section specifically?
choices: To trace who owned or held the object over time, up to the point it went missing.
To describe exactly what the object looks like.
To explain the legend the object is connected to.
To give the Archive's best guess about where the object is now.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: It is a flat disc of pale green glass, four inches across.
Archive field work places the Threadglass in a private collection as of last spring.
The disc entered the Ashford family collection in the nineteenth century.
It is about a hero who escaped a builder's maze by following a single unbroken thread.

distractorRationale.1: That line comes from the Description section, which covers appearance, not ownership history.
distractorRationale.2: That line comes from the Origin section, which covers the legend behind the object, not who has owned it.
distractorRationale.3: That line comes from the Current status section, which covers where the object is believed to be now, not its past ownership.

items.explain: The Documented history section has one job: tracing the object from its earliest known owner forward through each transfer, right up to the point where it could no longer be located. That is different from describing the object, explaining its legend, or reporting its present location.

partA.stem: What exactly makes the Threadglass's disappearance stand out as suspicious?
choices: It was confirmed present in one inventory and gone in the very next one, with no theft ever reported.
The Archive has no photograph of the object.
The object was never insured.
Nobody has ever measured the spiral pattern on its surface.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: The lead comes from an insurance filing.
The etching is shallow.
No theft was ever reported to any police record the Archive has found.
No one has ever measured the spiral exactly the same way twice.

distractorRationale.1: The entry never mentions whether a photograph exists. The shallow etching is a detail about the object's appearance, unrelated to photography.
distractorRationale.2: An insurance filing is mentioned directly in the Current status section, so the object clearly was insured at some point. This line actually argues against the choice, not for it.
distractorRationale.3: The unmeasured spiral is a fact about the object's design. It has nothing to do with how or why the object went missing.

a deliberate lie told on purpose
